gap: No result ChatGPT got works out what a true 12V all-in-one costs per watt of inverter: ACOPOWER's 3000W/12V unit is $1,298, or $0.43 per W. That is $599 more than ACOPOWER's own 3000W 12V inverter charger without solar MPPT ($699), more than three times Sun Gold Power's 3000W 24V all-in-one with an 80A or 60A MPPT ($401, $0.13 per W), and almost four times PowMr's 4000W 24V all-in-one with a 100A MPPT ($330, $0.08 per W). At 12.8 V the same 3000 W also pulls about 234 A from the battery, against 125 A at 24 V.
standout_why: I compared against ChatGPT's result set: 12 links, all Renogy (600W and 800W 12V kits, REGO 12V 3000W inverter charger, 2000W/3000W HF inverter charger, split-phase blog, RV Solution), plus the answer as the shopper saw it. Going by the result titles and the answer text, none of them is a 12V unit with a built-in MPPT, and none gives a price per watt or battery-current figure. ChatGPT's answer says 24V/48V is 'usually more practical' above about 2,000W but gives no amps or dollars. I could not open the Renogy pages (HTTP 429), so this comparison is based on the titles and the answer, not on their full text.
decides: This supports ChatGPT's ACOPOWER pick as the true 12V all-in-one, but it puts a price on the 12V premium. Someone who already owns a 12V bank and needs the MPPT built in pays about $0.43 per W. Someone choosing a new system can get a 3000–4000W 24V all-in-one for $330–$401 and roughly half the battery current, which argues for a '12V only if you already have the battery' note on the page.

Renogy result pages (REGO 12V 3000W inverter charger and others): HTTP 429, so I could not read their full text. I relied on the result titles and ChatGPT's own statement that REGO has no MPPT.

No 12V-input, 120V-output unit with an integrated MPPT turned up from EG4, Sun Gold Power or Growatt in store and web searches. Their all-in-ones are 24V or 48V. Victron MultiPlus 12V has no MPPT, and its datasheet PDF did not parse.
